title: OperatorSHAP: Fast and Accurate Shapley Value Estimation for Neural Operators
claim: Existing explainers are either slow or restricted to regular grids; ours is fast and works on any grid, with a real example.
layout: 2 panels: comparison table left, stacked heatmaps right; left-to-right
description: The left panel is a three-row comparison table with columns for method, inference speed, and grid flexibility. Classical SHAP (e.g., KernelSHAP) is slow but works on any grid. FastSHAP is fast but needs a homogeneous grid. OperatorSHAP is fast and works on any grid. The right panel has two stacked heatmaps of a cylinder-flow sample on an irregular triangular mesh. The top heatmap shows velocity magnitude in a viridis colormap, with a white circle for the cylinder and a small red star for the explained point. The bottom heatmap shows the OperatorSHAP attribution map in a red-white-blue diverging colormap. It has strong red regions upstream of and below the cylinder. Mesh points appear as small dots over both heatmaps. The eye goes first to the table, then to the colorful heatmaps.
caption: Left: Table with an overview of current methods. Right: A sample from the MeshGraphNets cylinder-flow dataset [ref]. Top shows a heatmap of airflow velocity strengths, with a grid of sensor points, and the cylinder object obstructing the airflow. The bottom shows the attribution map from OperatorSHAP for the same sample. The explained spatial point is marked with a red star. The varying cylinder placement in this dataset yields heterogeneous meshes, but OperatorSHAP is able to give correct explanations. Here, the area upstream of the cylinder and along its lower side is positively relevant, as the air flows from left to right.
abstract: Understanding model predictions is essential for physical applications, where outputs often inform safety-critical decisions, such as structural load assessment, weather warnings, and clinical diagnosis. Shapley values satisfy many desirable properties as an attribution method, but their computational cost during inference hinders their practical use. Current amortized explainers, such as FastSHAP, are limited to homogeneous inputs, which is problematic for physical applications where data often comes from irregular grids and geometries. We introduce OperatorSHAP, a grid-agnostic attribution method that allows us to train FastSHAP-like explainers for neural operators. We establish a theoretical framework for attributions in function space, connecting to Aumann-Shapley values. We further show that OperatorSHAP's explanations are consistent with state-of-the-art discrete Shapley values across resolutions and transfer across grid sizes without retraining.
